14a315d2882917a2.paragraph: This chapter establishes four theoretical foundations on which the rest of the thesis stands. Resource scheduling under a utilization lens (\Cref{sec:scheduling}) supplies the problem vocabulary and preloads efficiency; a five-layer human-in-the-loop theory (\Cref{sec:hitl}) supplies the configuration vocabulary and preloads trust/control; Transport Management Systems (\Cref{sec:tms}) position the category Ressursplanlegger sits inside and preload adaptability; and Design Science Research (\Cref{sec:dsr}) supplies the research paradigm under which an artefact-plus-knowledge contribution is built and investigated. Section length is asymmetric on purpose: \Cref{sec:hitl} carries the most argumentative load and is the longest, while Vehicle Routing theory inside \Cref{sec:scheduling} and TMS-as-category in \Cref{sec:tms} are referenced narrowly, the former to delimit, the latter to locate the planning gap the artefact fills. Because this is a bachelor's thesis, none of the four bodies is treated exhaustively: the chapter draws from each only as far as is needed to ground the choices made in RP and the claims made about it.
14a315d2882917a2.summary: Maps the chapter's four theoretical foundations to the three anchor concepts and explains why section lengths differ.

846bb9b39ca630d3.paragraph: The version of the problem RP solves is harder than the simplest single-resource case, because each transport assignment needs both a driver and a vehicle, and the two must stay paired for the whole assignment. In scheduling vocabulary, assignments are tasks with fixed time windows and fixed pickup-and-delivery locations, while drivers and vehicles are resources with their own attributes: a driver has competencies and availability, a vehicle has type and capacity. The planning horizon is dynamic: the coordinator sets it in the dashboard and can plan a single day, a week, or longer rotations as the company's operating rhythm requires. Pairing makes the problem harder than the single-resource case that dominates \parencite{pinedo2016scheduling}, because a candidate plan now has to satisfy compatibility for two resource types at the same moment, not one.
846bb9b39ca630d3.summary: Explains why pairing a driver and a vehicle makes RP's scheduling problem harder than the single-resource case.

366088132cad07b9.paragraph: Scheduling constraints are split into two kinds: hard and soft. Hard constraints must hold for a plan to be feasible at all: every driver-vehicle pairing has to be legally and physically capable of the assignment, and no resource may be double-booked. Concrete cases include the driver's licence class matching the vehicle, the driver holding any required certifications such as an ADR certificate for hazardous cargo, and the driver being on duty rather than on declared time-off. Soft constraints encode preferences the plan should honour where possible but may be traded off. Each is weighted in the objective function the solver tries to minimise. Examples include even workload across drivers, individual driver preferences, and continuity with the same customer over time. \textcite{ernst2004staff} state the rule directly: hard constraints must be satisfied while soft constraints may be violated, the latter entering the objective as penalty terms. \textcite{rossi2006constraint} say the same in constraint-programming vocabulary, distinguishing deadlines that bound feasibility from due dates that enter the weighted objective. The weights on soft constraints are configurable per company in RP, so a coordinator's notion of a good plan can be expressed without code changes.
366088132cad07b9.summary: Defines hard versus soft constraints and how RP handles each.

761a37fdd7a8da08.paragraph: Finding a guaranteed-best plan for a multi-resource assignment problem belongs to the class of NP-hard problems. NP-hard means that no algorithm is known that can solve every instance of the problem in time that grows polynomially with the size of the input, and one is widely believed not to exist. In practical terms, the time it takes to search every possible plan grows so fast as the number of drivers, vehicles, and assignments grows that exhaustive search stops being practical even on the daily fleets the interviewed companies operate, which range up to dozens of drivers and vehicles \parencite{rossi2006constraint, pinedo2016scheduling}. RP responds to this limit by giving up on provable optimality. Instead, the system uses solvers that return good plans within a time budget the coordinator sets, and \Cref{sec:iter-multiengine} describes how three different solvers were combined to do that. A different but adjacent literature, on Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs), addresses a related question: a VRP minimises total route cost over a sequence of customer visits delivered by a fleet from a depot \parencite{braekers2016vrp}, treating the order of stops as the main thing to decide. RP works on assignments with fixed locations and fixed time windows, so its open question is who performs each assignment, not in what order their stops are visited. \textcite{braekers2016vrp} explicitly exclude problems that combine routing with scheduling decisions from their review, which is the boundary RP sits on the scheduling side of.
761a37fdd7a8da08.summary: States the problem's NP-hardness and bounds RP against the adjacent Vehicle Routing Problem literature.

d4e9bae6d1e13e4d.paragraph: A traffic coordinator who reviews and approves every plan the algorithm produces is operating in what the human factors literature calls a human-in-the-loop configuration. The pattern is familiar from other domains. A nurse confirms a medication dose the system flags. A pilot accepts an autopilot suggestion before the autopilot acts. In each case an automated process generates a recommendation, and a human exercises authority over whether it takes effect. \textcite{parasuraman2000automation} formalise this on a ten-level scale of automation for decision and action selection. The scale runs from level 1 (fully manual) to level 10 (fully autonomous), with intermediate steps that progressively transfer authority from human to machine. Level 4 is "the computer suggests one alternative", level 5 is "executes that suggestion if the human approves", and level 6 is "executes automatically unless the human vetoes within a time window". RP sits at level 5: the solver produces one plan, the plan is shown on the timeline, and no driver is dispatched until the coordinator approves it. The artefact deliberately stops short of level 6: the coordinator must act, not merely fail to object.
d4e9bae6d1e13e4d.summary: Places RP at level 5 of Parasuraman's automation taxonomy and motivates partial human authority.

cd675670d5f47d3d.paragraph: Trust in the algorithm is a separate question from authority over it. A coordinator who has the authority to override the algorithm may still leave the system unused if they do not trust what it produces. \textcite{hoff2015trust} review 127 studies of human-automation trust from 101 articles, and group their findings into a three-layer model of dispositional, situational, and learned trust \parencite[p.~413]{hoff2015trust}. Dispositional trust reflects how much an individual tends to trust automation in general. Situational trust depends on context and workload. Learned trust is built through experience with the specific system: first as initial trust based on reputation, then as dynamic trust that updates with each interaction \parencite[p.~420]{hoff2015trust}. Two coordinators using the same plan generator may therefore hold different levels of trust at the same moment, and the same coordinator's reliance on the algorithm shifts across days. Hoff and Bashir also report that early errors damage trust more than later errors do \parencite[p.~426]{hoff2015trust}, which has a concrete consequence for deployment: a coordinator's first week with RP weighs more in trust formation than the months that follow. The studies the model rests on are mostly from aviation and military settings, so applying it to a small Norwegian coordinator pool is by analogy rather than direct empirical support. By analogy, the model gives the project not a number to predict but a design constraint: calibrated trust (neither over- nor under-reliance) is the target the artefact must enable through the override and explanation interfaces that the next two layers specify.
cd675670d5f47d3d.summary: Introduces Hoff and Bashir's three-layer trust model and what it means for deploying RP.

a1312dba51e472c1.paragraph: The fourth and deepest layer in HITL theory is a definition of trust itself. \textcite{lee2004trust} define trust as "the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual's goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability" \parencite[p.~54]{lee2004trust}, and argue that the design goal is appropriate trust, not greater trust. A coordinator who accepts every plan without review (over-reliance, what Lee and See call \textit{misuse}) and a coordinator who reverts to fully manual planning despite a competent solver (under-reliance, what they call \textit{disuse}) are both failures of trust calibration. Lee and See's design principles for trustable automation specify that the system should reveal its past performance, expose its process, and communicate its purpose in terms that connect to the user's goals \parencite[p.~74]{lee2004trust}. In RP, those three dimensions correspond to deviation history, scoring breakdown, and the explicit framing of the system as decision support rather than decision maker. The threat Lee and See identify is concrete. If coordinators do not understand or trust the algorithm, they will not adopt it, and the visibility gap §\ref{sec:scheduling} framed under efficiency will remain unaddressed regardless of solver quality. Chapter 5 returns to this adoption question.
a1312dba51e472c1.summary: Adopts Lee and See's definition of trust and the goal of appropriate, not maximal, trust calibration.

913979a669bb1faa.paragraph: Parasuraman's automation taxonomy, Hoff and Bashir's trust antecedents, Miller's explanation as interface, and Lee and See's definition of appropriate trust together translate into concrete design constraints on RP's HITL interface. The planning timeline at \texttt{/ressursplanlegger} shows the algorithm's suggested plan in the same Gantt view the coordinator uses for manual work, so the suggestion is open to inspection rather than presented as a finished output. After a solver run, a summary panel reports the solution score and counts of hard and soft violations, which exposes process and performance in the sense Lee and See describe. The deviation viewer at \texttt{/avvik} lists each active conflict by type, affected assignment, and affected resource, so a coordinator who disagrees with the algorithm can locate the contested assignment and decide whether to override. Override is intentionally low-friction: dragging an assignment block to a different employee row reassigns it, and conflicting changes save with a warning rather than a block. That choice is deliberate. A blocking validator would tell the coordinator that the system, not the coordinator, holds final authority, which is precisely the configuration Bainbridge warns against and the one Trust/control forbids. Soft constraints are weighted per company so that a coordinator's notion of a good plan can be adjusted without code changes, and the choice of solver engine and time budget is exposed at the point of plan generation so the system's capability limits are visible before the plan is read. These mechanisms are not features added to a finished automation. They are what makes the automation operable at all. \Cref{sec:iter-hitl,sec:iter-deviations,sec:iter-tradeoff} document how each layer was built into the artefact.
913979a669bb1faa.summary: Translates the four HITL theories into concrete RP interface mechanisms.

b323d51f02a5560d.paragraph: The first thing to establish about RP's environment is what kind of software the coordinator already works inside or alongside. Transport companies run their day-to-day operations on a category the industry groups under one label: a Transport Management System (TMS). \textcite{heinbach2022datadriven} define a TMS as software that plans and executes the physical movement of goods across supply chains \parencite[p.~811]{heinbach2022datadriven}, a definition the same authors trace back to TMS as freight-forwarder software for assigning customer shipments to fleet resources. \textcite{griffis2007tms} give a compatible definition from a North American shipper survey: a TMS is information technology used to plan, optimise, and execute transportation operations before, during, and after the physical movement of goods \parencite[p.~19]{griffis2007tms}. Across the rest of this section, "TMS" covers four operational areas: order management, route handling, carrier coordination, and freight billing.
b323d51f02a5560d.summary: Defines a Transport Management System as the software category transport companies operate within.

d39d248d13244347.paragraph: Even where a TMS is in place, one part of the operation is missing from the category as a whole: the upstream planning step that decides which driver and vehicle perform which assignment. \textcite{griffis2007tms} observe that most TMS offerings centre on the individual shipment as the unit of analysis and lack the ability to optimise multi-load shipments, leaving load consolidation as a manual activity \parencite[p.~27]{griffis2007tms}. \textcite{heinbach2022datadriven} reach the same conclusion: TMS products focus on shipment-level business activities, while other digital platforms add capabilities outside that focus \parencite[p.~808]{heinbach2022datadriven}. What existing systems cover, in short, is order management, freight billing, and shipment-level execution. What is missing is the upstream planning step between an order existing and a specific driver and vehicle being assigned to perform it. RP is positioned in exactly that gap. \Cref{chap:findings} substantiates the gap with the empirical comparison, and the per-company configurability that lets RP fit different vendor environments is built in \Cref{sec:iter-weights} and discussed under adaptability in §5.1.3. Section §\ref{sec:dsr} turns to the research paradigm under which an artefact filling the planning gap is built and investigated.
d39d248d13244347.summary: Names the upstream driver-and-vehicle planning gap that no TMS covers and that RP fills.

4cdb851135eb1697.paragraph: Design Science Research (DSR) is the research paradigm in which a designed artefact is constructed and investigated as the central contribution of a study, together with the knowledge produced about how that artefact behaves in its context. The point is that the artefact and the knowledge come out of the same project. \textcite{wieringa2014dsm} states the position concisely: design science is the design and investigation of artefacts in context, where the artefact is built to improve something in its problem context \parencite[p.~3]{wieringa2014dsm}. \textcite{hevner2007threecycle} structures the same work as three linked cycles. The relevance cycle imports requirements and acceptance criteria from the application environment. The rigor cycle draws on the existing scientific knowledge base and contributes new knowledge back to it. The design cycle iterates internally between constructing and evaluating the artefact \parencite[pp.~88--90]{hevner2007threecycle}. \textcite{peffers2007dsrm} structure the same paradigm as a procedural model. Their Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) specifies six activities: problem identification and motivation; objectives for a solution; design and development; demonstration; evaluation; and communication \parencite[p.~46]{peffers2007dsrm}. The two framings are complementary: the cycles describe what must be present, the activities describe what is done. Chapter 3 applies the DSRM activities step by step to this project.
4cdb851135eb1697.summary: Defines Design Science Research as artefact-plus-knowledge construction via Hevner's cycles and Peffers' six activities.

faa36ebe341e7876.paragraph: DSR is not the only research paradigm available for an information systems study, and two alternatives in the IS literature warrant comparison. \textcite{orlikowski1991studying} survey the IS literature and group it into three philosophical stances: positivist, interpretive, and critical \parencite[p.~5]{orlikowski1991studying}. The positivist stance assumes an objective social reality investigated with structured instruments, with the goal of testing hypotheses to increase predictive understanding \parencite[p.~5]{orlikowski1991studying}. That stance fits a study that measures population-level effects of a deployed system, but on its own it cannot justify building a new artefact whose primary contribution is the design knowledge embedded in it. The interpretive stance assumes that organisational reality is socially constructed and seeks contextual understanding through participants' meanings rather than generalisable laws \parencite[p.~5]{orlikowski1991studying}. That stance fits a study whose contribution is rich description of coordinator practice, but on its own it cannot support building a runnable artefact whose behaviour can be checked against external criteria. DSR is the third paradigm the present project requires: an artefact-plus-knowledge contribution in which qualitative input informs requirements, and the artefact itself is examined against those requirements.
faa36ebe341e7876.summary: Compares positivist and interpretive paradigms to justify why DSR fits this artefact-plus-knowledge project.

06bad32d905e36eb.paragraph: Inside DSR, the distinction between validation and evaluation shapes what kind of empirical evidence the project can offer. \textcite{wieringa2014dsm} distinguishes validation from evaluation. Validation predicts whether a deployed system would do what stakeholders want; evaluation observes a deployed system in actual use \parencite[p.~31]{wieringa2014dsm}. In validation, the researcher experiments with a model of how stakeholders would use the artefact. In evaluation, stakeholders use the artefact independently of the researcher \parencite[p.~34]{wieringa2014dsm}. The present thesis validates rather than evaluates RP. Behaviour is predicted in two ways. The first is benchmarking on synthetic datasets, which is a single-case mechanism experiment in Wieringa's classification (one artefact, controlled inputs) \parencite[p.~64]{wieringa2014dsm}. The second is requirements traceability against the requirements derived in the relevance cycle. No transport company has operated the system independently. \textcite{hevner2007threecycle} treats this exact ordering as expected practice, with artefacts tested in laboratory and experimental situations before being released into field testing along the relevance cycle \parencite[p.~91]{hevner2007threecycle}, so the absence of production deployment is a structural feature of the project's stage rather than a methodological deficit. \Cref{sec:evaluation-framework} applies this distinction to the synthetic-benchmark protocol, and Section 5.4 returns to it as limitation L5 when bounding what that validation can and cannot claim.
06bad32d905e36eb.summary: Distinguishes Wieringa's validation from evaluation and explains why this thesis validates rather than evaluates RP.

42f8bc235b782d3b.paragraph: Improving Efficiency is not possible without first being able to see it. A coordinator working from a spreadsheet or whiteboard cannot reduce overtime they cannot count, or balance a workload they cannot view across drivers. Before the system reorders any assignment, its first contribution is putting those utilization measures in front of the coordinator in a single view they can read at a glance.
42f8bc235b782d3b.summary: Argues that visibility of utilization measures is the artefact's first contribution, before any reordering.

ad5bccc996447ef0.paragraph: Scheduling constraints split into two kinds, hard and soft, which the solver treats differently. Hard constraints must hold for a plan to be feasible at all: every driver-vehicle pairing has to be legally and physically capable of the assignment, and no resource may be double-booked. Concrete cases include the driver's licence class matching the vehicle, the driver holding any required certifications such as an ADR certificate for hazardous cargo, and the driver being on duty rather than on declared time-off. \textcite{ernst2004staff} state the rule directly: hard constraints must be satisfied; \textcite{rossi2006constraint} say the same in constraint-programming vocabulary, distinguishing deadlines that bound feasibility from due dates that enter the weighted objective.
ad5bccc996447ef0.summary: Defines hard constraints as feasibility requirements with concrete licence and double-booking examples.

11947622fdfae971.paragraph: Constructive heuristics, called dispatching rules in \textcite{pinedo2016scheduling}, build a plan one assignment at a time according to a priority rule, for example ``schedule the most constrained job first''. They are fast, but they can lock onto a locally good plan and miss a much better plan that would only be reachable by reordering earlier choices.
11947622fdfae971.summary: Describes constructive heuristics as fast, priority-rule-driven solvers that can lock onto locally good plans.

11ff43004c8a22e4.paragraph: Constraint programming formalises the problem as variables and constraints and then searches the space of feasible plans systematically. It uses propagation, which deduces forced choices from the constraints, and backtracking, which undoes a choice that leads to a dead end. Within a time budget the solver returns near-optimal plans, at the cost of higher modelling effort upfront \parencite{rossi2006constraint}.
11ff43004c8a22e4.summary: Describes constraint programming as systematic search with propagation and backtracking under a time budget.

6180d1334fdcc244.paragraph: Metaheuristics are general-purpose search strategies that improve a current candidate plan by repeatedly modifying it. Two well-known examples illustrate the family. The tabu search of \textcite{glover1986future} keeps a short-term memory of recent moves to avoid cycling back to them. The late-acceptance hill climbing of \textcite{burke2017late} accepts a new candidate if it is no worse than the candidate seen a fixed number of steps ago. Both let the search escape locally good plans on large instances.
6180d1334fdcc244.summary: Describes metaheuristics through tabu search and late-acceptance hill climbing as escape mechanisms on large instances.

The scale runs from level 1 (fully manual) to level 10 (fully autonomous), with intermediate steps that progressively transfer authority from human to machine. Level 4 is ``the computer suggests one alternative'', level 5 is ``executes that suggestion if the human approves'', and level 6 is ``executes automatically unless the human vetoes within a time window''. RP sits at level 5: the solver produces one plan, the plan is shown on the timeline, and no driver is dispatched until the coordinator approves it. The artefact deliberately stops short of level 6, where the coordinator would only need to fail to object.
4a0559bb9a3db117.summary: Places RP at level 5 of Parasuraman's ten-level automation taxonomy.

1dcd6e2eb8e0304d.paragraph: Inside that label, the picture is not uniform. What a TMS actually offers depends on the vendor, and whether a transport company uses one at all depends on the company. In the Norwegian market, the two commercial systems named in the interviews are \textbf{Timpex} and \textbf{Opter}. Both cover order management and freight billing, and neither generates assignment plans automatically. Adoption itself is uneven. \textcite{griffis2007tms} report that of the firms in their 2007 North American sample without any TMS, half manage transportation entirely manually, while the other half rely on partial or legacy IT \parencite[p.~26]{griffis2007tms}. The sector RP enters is therefore a patchwork: different vendors cover different ground, and a substantial share of operations run without dedicated planning software at all.
1dcd6e2eb8e0304d.summary: Shows that TMS coverage varies by vendor and that adoption itself is uneven across the sector.

6f1045c94d4dfec6.summary: Names the upstream driver-and-vehicle planning gap that no TMS covers and that RP fills.

b8de8ba7915b58f3.paragraph: \textcite{hevner2007threecycle} structures the same work as three linked cycles. The relevance cycle imports requirements and acceptance criteria from the application environment. The rigor cycle draws on the existing scientific knowledge base and contributes new knowledge back to it. The design cycle iterates internally between constructing and evaluating the artefact \parencite[pp.~88--90]{hevner2007threecycle}.
b8de8ba7915b58f3.summary: Presents Hevner's three-cycle structure of relevance, rigor, and design.

4f740ce4b7123b19.paragraph: \textcite{peffers2007dsrm} structure the same paradigm as a procedural model. Their Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) specifies six activities: problem identification and motivation; objectives for a solution; design and development; demonstration; evaluation; and communication \parencite[p.~46]{peffers2007dsrm}. The two framings are complementary: the cycles describe what must be present, the activities describe what is done. \Cref{chap:method} applies the DSRM activities step by step to this project.
4f740ce4b7123b19.summary: Presents Peffers' DSRM as six procedural activities and notes complementarity with Hevner's cycles.

17ac5e607cfdd2be.paragraph: This chapter develops four theoretical foundations the rest of the thesis stands on. \Cref{sec:scheduling} sets out the scheduling problem the algorithm solves and names the utilization dimensions grouped under \textbf{Efficiency}. \Cref{sec:hitl} sets out the human-in-the-loop pattern under which the coordinator runs the system, and names \textbf{Trust/control} as a structural requirement of that pattern. \Cref{sec:tms} places RP inside the existing software category and identifies the planning gap RP fills. \Cref{sec:dsr} sets out the research paradigm that frames both the artefact and the knowledge claims made about it. Of the four, \Cref{sec:hitl} carries the most theoretical weight: the trust-and-control argument the rest of the thesis turns on is built there.
17ac5e607cfdd2be.summary: Previews the four theoretical foundations of the chapter and flags HITL as the load-bearing one.

1fefebd1007a6eda.paragraph: The three families differ along two axes that matter for RP: speed (how quickly they return a candidate plan) and quality (how close that plan is to optimal). Heuristics are fastest but can lock in early; constraint programming searches systematically but takes longer to set up; metaheuristics keep improving as long as time allows. RP runs all three behind one interface, and the coordinator chooses the speed-quality trade-off at the point of plan generation. \Cref{sec:iter-multiengine} reports how each engine behaves on the same benchmark instances. Solver capability alone, however, says nothing about who reads the resulting plan, who can change it, and on what authority. \Cref{sec:hitl} turns to that question.
1fefebd1007a6eda.summary: Frames the speed-versus-quality trade-off and notes that RP exposes all three engines behind one interface.

6089fb7104b203ce.paragraph: A nurse confirms a medication dose the hospital system flags. A pilot accepts an autopilot suggestion before the autopilot acts. In each case an automated process generates a recommendation, and a human exercises authority over whether it takes effect. The human factors literature calls this configuration human-in-the-loop. A traffic coordinator who reviews and approves every plan the algorithm produces is operating in exactly the same pattern.
6089fb7104b203ce.summary: Introduces human-in-the-loop through familiar examples and locates the coordinator inside the same pattern.

13863a11c392f8c5.paragraph: For the coordinator to trust the algorithm in a way that matches how good it actually is, they need to understand what it is doing. \textcite{miller2019explanation} surveys explanation in the social sciences and notes three things most automated systems get wrong. First, explanations are contrastive: when people ask why something happened, they usually mean why it happened rather than the alternative they had in mind. Second, explanations are selective: people want one or two key reasons, not the full causal chain. Third, explanations are social: explaining is a kind of communication, so a good explanation fits what the listener already knows \parencite[p.~3]{miller2019explanation}. Translated to a planning algorithm, the coordinator's question is rarely ``why was this assignment generated?''. It is ``why was this driver assigned, rather than the one I would have picked?''. Miller argues that explanation belongs in the interface itself, and that ``trust is lost when users cannot understand traces of observed behaviour or decisions'' \parencite[p.~3]{miller2019explanation}. The implication for RP is that the system has to give reasons in the coordinator's vocabulary (competence, time, current load), not in raw constraint weights and solver internals, and those reasons belong next to the override controls themselves.
13863a11c392f8c5.summary: Applies Miller's contrastive, selective, social account of explanation to what RP must show next to overrides.

d08f5ce7398e8f80.paragraph: \textcite{lee2004trust} define trust as the user's belief that the system will help them reach their goals in a situation where they cannot fully predict what it will do \parencite[p.~54]{lee2004trust}. Their key argument is that the design goal is the right amount of trust, not the maximum amount. A coordinator who accepts every plan without checking it (Lee and See call this \textit{misuse}) is over-trusting; a coordinator who plans entirely by hand even when the solver works well (\textit{disuse}) is under-trusting. To help a user calibrate, Lee and See recommend that the system reveal its past performance, show how it works, and explain its purpose in terms that connect to the user's goals \parencite[p.~74]{lee2004trust}. The risk Lee and See point to is concrete: if coordinators do not understand or trust the algorithm, they will not use it, and the visibility gap from \Cref{sec:scheduling} stays open regardless of how good the solver is. \Cref{chap:discussion} returns to this adoption question.
d08f5ce7398e8f80.summary: Introduces Lee and See's appropriate-trust definition with misuse and disuse as the two failure modes.

3f9ef9864d4da06b.paragraph: The four bodies above (Parasuraman's automation taxonomy, Hoff and Bashir's trust antecedents, Miller's explanation as interface, and Lee and See's definition of appropriate trust) translate into concrete design constraints on RP's HITL interface. The planning timeline shows the algorithm's suggested plan in the same Gantt view the coordinator uses for manual work, so the suggestion is open to inspection rather than presented as a finished output. After a solver run, a summary panel reports the solution score and counts of hard and soft violations, exposing process and performance in the sense Lee and See describe. A separate deviation view lists each active conflict by type, affected assignment, and affected resource, so a coordinator who disagrees with the algorithm can locate the contested assignment and decide whether to override. Override is intentionally low-friction: dragging an assignment block to a different employee row reassigns it, and conflicting changes save with a warning rather than a block. A blocking validator would tell the coordinator that the system, not the coordinator, holds final authority, which is the configuration Bainbridge warns against and the one \textbf{Trust/control} forbids. Soft-constraint weights are exposed per company so that a coordinator's notion of a good plan can be adjusted without code changes, and the choice of solver engine and time budget is exposed at the point of plan generation so the system's capability limits are visible before the plan is read. \Cref{sec:iter-hitl,sec:iter-deviations,sec:iter-tradeoff} document how each layer was built into the artefact.
3f9ef9864d4da06b.summary: Translates the four HITL theories into RP's concrete interface decisions for inspection, override, and configuration.
3f9ef9864d4da06b.feedback: Should this paragraph be here? isnt theory just theory?

186ced979410886f.paragraph: Even where a TMS is in place, one part of the operation is missing from the category as a whole: the upstream planning step that decides which driver and vehicle perform which assignment. \textcite{griffis2007tms} observe that most TMS offerings centre on the individual shipment as the unit of analysis and lack the ability to optimise multi-load shipments, leaving load consolidation as a manual activity \parencite[p.~27]{griffis2007tms}. \textcite{heinbach2022datadriven} reach the same conclusion: TMS products focus on shipment-level business activities, while other digital platforms add capabilities outside that focus \parencite[p.~808]{heinbach2022datadriven}. What existing systems cover, in short, is order management, freight billing, and shipment-level execution; what is missing is the upstream planning step between an order existing and a specific driver and vehicle being assigned to perform it. RP is positioned in exactly that gap. \Cref{chap:findings} substantiates the gap with the empirical comparison, and the per-company configurability that lets RP fit different vendor environments is built in \Cref{sec:iter-weights} and discussed under \textbf{Adaptability} in §5.1.3. \Cref{sec:dsr} turns to the research paradigm under which an artefact filling that gap is built and investigated.
186ced979410886f.summary: Identifies the upstream driver-and-vehicle planning step as the gap RP is positioned to fill.

b481ae93989bb54d.paragraph: The hard and soft constraints introduced in \Cref{sec:problem} are formalised in scheduling theory as follows. Hard constraints bound feasibility: a plan that violates one is not a valid plan. Each violated soft constraint adds a penalty to the score the solver tries to minimise \parencite{ernst2004staff, rossi2006constraint}, so the solver searches for a plan that respects every hard constraint and incurs the smallest total soft-constraint penalty. The size of each penalty is a weight set per company in RP, so a coordinator's notion of a good plan can be expressed without code changes.
b481ae93989bb54d.feedback: weight needs introduction if not introduced in ch1.

65944810822f52d4.paragraph: Producing a plan that legally fits every assignment is one bar; producing one that uses the company's drivers and vehicles well is a different one, and harder. The personnel-scheduling literature judges plans on these utilization dimensions, in particular overtime hours, idle time, and workload balance \parencite{ernst2004staff}. None of these can improve before the coordinator can see them: the system's first contribution, as \Cref{sec:problem} previewed, is putting them in front of the coordinator in a single view they can read at a glance.
65944810822f52d4.feedback: 1. Reword to match Ernst's vocabulary. Change "overtime hours, idle time between assignments, and how evenly the workload spreads" to "cost, employee preferences, and equitable workload distribution" — Ernst's own four objectives. Direct citation, clean.

3f1fc5d9b0973b56.paragraph: Consider a small transport business consisting of one owner-operator and one vehicle. The work is straightforward at the outset. When a customer calls with goods to be moved, the operator checks the calendar, accepts the job if time is available, and turns it down if it is not. One delivery follows another, and the day arranges itself around what comes in.
3f1fc5d9b0973b56.summary: Chapter intro vignette + sector context, currently nested inside §1.1 The Problem.

f363ee82bc42afeb.context: Methodology > Method Theory: DSR + DSRM Applied
f363ee82bc42afeb.paragraph: The methodology used in this thesis is \textcite{peffers2007dsrm}'s Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM), which structures DSR as six activities: problem identification and motivation, objectives for a solution, design and development, demonstration, evaluation, and communication \parencite[p.~46]{peffers2007dsrm}. Peffers note that the activities are nominally sequential rather than strictly so; researchers are not expected to walk in order from activity 1 through activity 6 \parencite[p.~56]{peffers2007dsrm}.
f363ee82bc42afeb.summary: DSRM structures DSR as six nominally sequential activities; researchers are not expected to walk them strictly in order.

d12d55a0f9cdbad8.paragraph: The interviews were conducted as an industry consultation, not as formal academic research, and that framing has ethical consequences worth stating directly. The project ran under Admmit's bachelor task brief and NTNU institutional supervision, and on that basis no Sikt registration was sought. (Sikt is Norway's national agency for shared services in research and education.) The conversations covered work practices, system use, and assignment criteria only. No special-category personal data was collected. Special-category here is the GDPR term for sensitive data such as health, ethnicity, and political views; none of that was discussed. Consent was implicit: participants agreed to take the call and answer questions. The consultation framing makes that acceptable given the absence of sensitive data and the professional context, but no formal consent form was administered, and recording proceeded without an explicit pre-recording consent step. No formal anonymisation protocol was applied for the same reason: the seven coordinators are professionals speaking about their working practices, not research participants whose personal data is being processed. Only Timpex and Opter, the two commercial vendors named in the consultation pool, are named in the thesis. The seven interviewed companies are referenced generically by size, sector, and system maturity. Recordings and transcriptions are stored locally on the project author's device, accessible only to the author and supervisor, and will be deleted after submission and grading. The researcher--developer overlap and the informal study procedures that follow from this consultation framing are named together as L3 in \Cref{sec:limitations}.
d12d55a0f9cdbad8.summary: Interviews were treated as industry consultation under NTNU supervision: no Sikt registration, implicit consent, no special-category data.
d12d55a0f9cdbad8.feedback:
Real ethical clarity needed before a clean rewrite is possible. Two sentences hedge:
(1) 'On that basis no Sikt registration was sought.' Did NTNU institutional supervision confirm this, or did the team decide based on the consultation framing? If NTNU confirmed: state it directly ('After consultation with NTNU institutional supervision, no Sikt registration was sought'). If the team decided unilaterally: state that, and L3 in §5.4 needs to carry the weight.
(2) 'Recording proceeded without an explicit pre-recording consent step.' Did participants know they were being recorded? If yes (verbal at recording time): say so -- that is verbal consent and worth naming. If no: that is a real problem and L3 must carry it.
Until those two facts are clear, suggestion left null. Tighten the order so the conditions justify the implicit consent in the same sentence once facts are settled.

aa9e110219434c8f.context: Methodology > Iterative Development Process > Configurable Soft-constraint Weights
aa9e110219434c8f.paragraph:
\begin{description}
  \item[Origin.] Designer and architectural. The iteration delivers the Adaptability anchor that the project committed to from the start through the Admmit-mandated multi-tenant architecture. The specific weight set was chosen by the designers, not interview-validated as the right set.
  \item[Tried.] A per-company weight configuration UI for soft constraints: workload balance, vehicle preference, transitions between consecutive assignments, priority, and employee preferences. Each weight flows into the CP-SAT objective function so that the same engine produces different plans for different companies without code changes.
  \item[Why.] The interviews confirmed that assignment criteria differ materially across companies. Some companies weight workload balance highly. Others prioritise vehicle--driver continuity or route familiarity. Adaptability means the same artefact must serve materially different operational rules within a single deployed instance.
  \item[What happened.] User-chosen weight combinations were hard to validate against pathological cases. Weights summing to zero produced unstable rankings, and one weight dominating the others produced plans that satisfied a single criterion at the cost of all others. The user-experience (UX) challenge was explaining what each weight actually means to a coordinator who does not work in optimisation vocabulary.
  \item[Learned.] Configurability for soft weights is a partial realisation of Adaptability. Hard constraints, status workflow definitions, and per-company assignment-rule taxonomies remain hard-coded; broader configurability of those layers is named as a gap in \Cref{sec:limitations} and forwarded to future work in \Cref{sec:future-work}.
  \item[Next.] With eight iterations of artefact in place, the methodological question becomes how to test whether the artefact meets the locked anchors. That question is answered in \Cref{sec:evaluation-framework}.
\end{description}
aa9e110219434c8f.summary: Iteration 8 added per-company configurable soft-constraint weights, partially realising the Adaptability anchor.

79782ea0a5a1b596.paragraph: Admmit, a Norwegian software firm building products for the transport sector, offered a bachelor task through NTNU under project code OPG29. The task description asked for a working prototype of a planning platform that could help Norwegian traffic coordinators assign drivers and vehicles to the day's transport assignments. The two-student team accepted the task and committed to delivering both the artefact, named RP, and the thesis that surrounds it. From that point onwards, two workstreams ran in parallel: building the platform and conducting the research that would inform its design.
79782ea0a5a1b596.summary: Admmit gave NTNU a bachelor task; the two-student team accepted and ran build and research workstreams in parallel.

0eaf7ffb53b1d792.paragraph: The task description fixed the topic but not the empirical foundation, and the team needed answers before any planning interface could be designed responsibly. Two questions in particular: how do Norwegian traffic coordinators actually plan a day's assignments, and what software, if any, do they use today? Neither question could be answered from the desk. The team turned to Admmit's customer roster, called seven traffic coordinators and transport managers directly, and conducted brief semi-structured calls of roughly fifteen minutes each. The calls were spread across the first half of March 2026 rather than compressed into one day; each call was conducted on its own, and the team adjusted prompts and reflected between calls so that gaps in earlier conversations could be probed in later ones. Vendor names surfaced gradually through "what tools do you use" questions: several companies described mixes rather than single-vendor adoption, with Timpex, Opter, and internal tools appearing in different combinations across the seven companies interviewed.
0eaf7ffb53b1d792.summary: Seven coordinators were called in March 2026 to learn how planning is done today and which tools they use.
0eaf7ffb53b1d792.feedback: dont mention 7 directly ever in the bachelros thesis.

d84a64a974f57556.paragraph: Admmit had already specified two requirements before the first call. The first was Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) operation: the algorithm proposes a plan, and the coordinator can review and override every assignment in it. The second was a multi-tenant architecture, meaning one deployed system serving several customer companies, with each company's data and configuration isolated from the others. The seven coordinators voiced a clear preference for a system that suggests a plan they can correct rather than one that decides for them, which matched the HITL requirement. Their accounts of differing operational rules across companies matched the case for the multi-tenant architecture. Admmit had the requirements; the seven companies interviewed validated them.
d84a64a974f57556.summary: Admmit had pre-specified HITL and multi-tenant requirements; the seven interviewed coordinators validated both.

e519f92230a6a351.paragraph: The seven coordinators were selected purposively from Admmit's customer roster rather than through a public call. The project required coordinators in the planning role at companies where algorithm-assisted planning is plausibly relevant, and Admmit's customer base supplied that population directly. The companies span small operators with around eight to twenty drivers up to a multi-department fleet of around forty-five vehicles, range geographically from Bergen and Mo i Rana to Lakselv and Tana, and cover the systems used in the field: Timpex, Opter, internal or custom tools, and fully manual planning. The self-selection that follows from recruiting through Admmit's customer roster is a known limitation on the empirical foundation, named as L2 in \Cref{sec:limitations}.
e519f92230a6a351.summary: Coordinators were purposively recruited from Admmit's customer roster, spanning fleet size, geography, and system maturity.

3d8122bf17f37cc5.paragraph: The seven calls were conducted by phone across the first half of March 2026, in Norwegian. Each call lasted approximately fifteen minutes, for a cumulative interview time of roughly 105 minutes. The calls were spread across multiple days rather than compressed into one window, so the team could adjust prompts between calls and probe gaps in earlier conversations later on. Phone was the practical choice given the geographic spread of the coordinators (Bergen, Mo i Rana, Lakselv, Tana) and the brief format the consultation could realistically ask of working coordinators recruited cold. Norwegian was chosen as the working language because all seven coordinators were native speakers, and the topic vocabulary (TMS terminology, regulatory references, sick-leave handling) is naturally expressed in Norwegian. The fifteen-minute target balanced cross-topic coverage against the realistic attention budget of a working day. The brief duration is named alongside the sample size as L1 in \Cref{sec:limitations}.
3d8122bf17f37cc5.summary: Calls were conducted by phone in Norwegian over March 2026, fifteen minutes each, with brief duration named as L1.

65a7949e7cb2aec9.paragraph: Thematic analysis was the approach the team used to turn the interview audio into themes the project could act on. \textcite{braun2006thematic} present thematic analysis (TA) as a flexible qualitative method that codes statements into themes through repeated readings of the material. It was chosen for its theoretical flexibility within the DSR frame \parencite[p.~81]{braun2006thematic} and its accessibility to a small research team conducting analysis as one component of a larger DSR Problem-Identification activity \parencite[p.~77]{braun2006thematic}. The analysis was conducted in the six phases Braun and Clarke specify: familiarisation, initial coding, theme search, theme review, theme definition, and report production \parencite[p.~87]{braun2006thematic}.
65a7949e7cb2aec9.summary: Thematic analysis was chosen for its flexibility within DSR, conducted in Braun and Clarke's six phases.

eff00f59dec03bcf.paragraph: Braun and Clarke's own examples are drawn from psychology and gender studies. The application here is to brief semi-structured consultations with traffic coordinators inside a DSR Problem-Identification activity, not to standalone qualitative research. The six-phase guide transfers across that domain gap by treating each transcript as a data item and the seven transcripts together as the data set.
eff00f59dec03bcf.summary: Braun and Clarke's six-phase guide transfers from psychology and gender studies to brief consultations inside a DSR Problem-Identification activity.

e6a38563db1bf1c6.paragraph: The analysis carries the limitations of its inputs and its frame, named as L1 and L2 in \Cref{sec:data-collection} and catalogued in full in \Cref{sec:limitations}. The themes are accordingly bounded to the seven interviewed companies and are not a basis for generalising to Norwegian transport more broadly.
e6a38563db1bf1c6.summary: The analysis carries the L1 and L2 limitations of its inputs and is bounded to the seven interviewed companies.

299a8d7a2abe5fab.context: Methodology > Iterative Development Process > Schema and Timeline Scaffolding
299a8d7a2abe5fab.paragraph:
\begin{description}
  \item[Origin.] Admmit-mandate (multi-tenant architecture) combined with designer-technical exploration of the data model and a read-only timeline UI (user interface).
  \item[Tried.] A core entity model covering employees, vehicles, assignments, certifications, weekly work schedules, and time-off. Multi-tenant data isolation was enforced at the data layer, with every query scoped by \texttt{companyId}. A read-only Gantt-style timeline rendered existing assignments without any optimisation step.
  \item[Why.] Later solver iterations need a structured substrate to operate over. The multi-tenant boundary must be enforced at the data layer because Admmit's customer structure means each transport company would consume the artefact independently; bolting tenancy on later would risk cross-tenant leakage on every new query path.
  \item[What happened.] The substrate was adequate for the simplest assignment heuristic but required revision once constraint-solver formalisation exposed gaps in the data model. Explicit time-off windows, certificate-expiry as a queryable date, and per-day work-schedule entries became necessary only after the heuristic showed what the solver would need to reason about.
  \item[Learned.] Schema-first discipline reduces rework but cannot fully anticipate solver requirements. The substrate is itself an iteration, not a one-shot setup.
  \item[Next.] With the substrate stable enough to support a real assignment step, the next iteration attempted the simplest possible assignment heuristic.
\end{description}
299a8d7a2abe5fab.summary: Iteration 1 built the multi-tenant data substrate and a read-only Gantt timeline before any solver step.

6edd77ffa1dafe73.context: Methodology > Iterative Development Process > Single-engine Baseline (greedy)
6edd77ffa1dafe73.paragraph:
\begin{description}
  \item[Origin.] Designer-technical exploration.
  \item[Tried.] A priority-sorted greedy first-fit assignment heuristic. Assignments were sorted by priority, walked through in order, and each was given the first feasible driver and vehicle combination found.
  \item[Why.] An instant baseline that produces a feasible plan provides a reference point for measuring richer-solver gains, and gives the coordinator immediate feedback while drag-and-drop edits happen.
  \item[What happened.] The heuristic worked on small instances of fewer than thirty assignments. On larger instances, priority-sorted greedy committed early to locally optimal but globally suboptimal choices, blocking later high-priority assignments and producing avoidable idle time and overtime.
  \item[Learned.] The greedy heuristic's quality limit is structural rather than tunable: reordering the priority comparator cannot break out of it because the heuristic lacks both constraint propagation and a global view of the day.
  \item[Next.] Introduce a complete solver that can reason about all assignments simultaneously.
\end{description}
6edd77ffa1dafe73.summary: Iteration 2 implemented a priority-sorted greedy heuristic, which committed early and produced avoidable idle time on larger instances.

4bf7ee7d0767db91.context: Methodology > Iterative Development Process > Constraint Generalisation (CP-SAT)
4bf7ee7d0767db91.paragraph:
\begin{description}
  \item[Origin.] Designer-technical exploration.
  \item[Tried.] The Google OR-Tools CP-SAT solver with explicit hard constraints (competencies, availability, no double-booking, vehicle type) and weighted soft constraints (workload balance, vehicle preference, transitions, priority, employee preferences) combined under an objective function that maximises scheduled assignments minus weighted soft-constraint violations.
  \item[Why.] Constraint programming is well-suited to assignment problems with combinations of hard and soft constraints, and CP-SAT specifically returns near-optimal solutions within a configurable time budget. That property matters for an HITL interface where the coordinator is waiting on the solver.
  \item[What happened.] The solver returned near-optimal solutions on small to medium instances within a thirty-to-sixty-second time limit. Quality degraded on larger instances when the time limit bound: the solver returned the best feasible solution found rather than the optimum. Modelling complexity was higher than for the heuristic, and several iterations were needed to get the hard-versus-soft mapping correct.
  \item[Learned.] CP-SAT covers the medium-instance gap that the greedy heuristic could not, but introduces a scaling boundary that motivates a third engine for larger instances.
  \item[Next.] Add a third engine for large instances and a mechanism for comparing the three under matched conditions.
\end{description}
4bf7ee7d0767db91.summary: Iteration 3 added an OR-Tools CP-SAT solver with explicit hard and weighted soft constraints under a single objective function.

a2bb708fb97eb815.context: Methodology > Iterative Development Process > HITL Interface
a2bb708fb97eb815.paragraph:
\begin{description}
  \item[Origin.] Mixed: Admmit-mandate combined with interview-validated direction. The drag-and-drop interaction style was confirmed by coordinator consensus that the system should suggest a plan the coordinator can correct, not replace the coordinator.
  \item[Tried.] A Gantt-style drag-and-drop assignment UI, an explicit inspect / modify / accept / reject control on every algorithm-generated suggestion, and a thin post-hoc constraint check that flagged basic feasibility violations such as over-booking and missing competence.
  \item[Why.] HITL was Admmit's requirement from project start, and the interviews validated the necessity through a coordinator consensus that automated planning must be correctable rather than authoritative. Without an interactive override path, the coordinator would have authority in principle but no way to exercise it on the timeline they actually work with.
  \item[What happened.] Drag-and-drop worked. State consistency between optimistic UI updates and server mutations occasionally produced stale conflict displays, where the timeline showed a violation the server had already resolved, and required a refresh hook on assignment updates. The thin post-hoc check caught the most common conflicts but was clearly insufficient for the range of edge cases the coordinator would encounter.
  \item[Learned.] The HITL interface needs richer real-time feedback than a thin post-hoc check provides. Coordinator authority over plan content is meaningful only when the system shows what to act on; an empty timeline the coordinator edits blindly delivers Trust/control only on paper.
  \item[Next.] Expand the post-hoc check into a full deviation taxonomy that materialises the constraints the coordinator would otherwise have to remember.
\end{description}
a2bb708fb97eb815.summary: Iteration 5 built the Gantt drag-and-drop HITL interface with a thin post-hoc constraint check that proved insufficient.

8e68971741962863.paragraph: The framework that tests RP's claims is asymmetric on purpose. Some claims are tested directly, through the multi-engine benchmark; others are accepted as inputs the framework does not itself test, following the position carried through \Cref{sec:iter-multiengine}.
8e68971741962863.summary: The evaluation framework is asymmetric on purpose: some claims are tested directly, others are accepted as inputs.

4d893e3826f2806b.paragraph: Each of the three anchors is tested to a different extent, and the coverage is asymmetric across them. \textbf{Efficiency} is the most directly tested anchor. The multi-engine benchmark is the validation instrument designed for it, comparing scheduled-assignment count, soft-constraint penalty, and runtime-within-budget across the greedy heuristic, OR-Tools CP-SAT, and Timefold metaheuristic on identical problem instances. \textbf{Adaptability} is tested only indirectly. The requirements traceability matrix records that the per-company configurable weight interface (\Cref{sec:iter-weights}) is implemented and verified during development, but no benchmark compares the artefact's behaviour across two genuinely different operational rulebooks. \textbf{Trust/control} is also tested only partially. The inspect / modify / accept / reject flow is implemented, but it has not been user-tested with traffic coordinators, and that gap is forwarded to L8 in \Cref{sec:limitations}.
4d893e3826f2806b.summary: Efficiency is tested directly through the multi-engine benchmark; Adaptability and Trust/control are tested only indirectly or partially.

9d978b7b68a9873b.paragraph: The requirements traceability matrix is the coverage check rather than a quality validation. For each functional requirement in the FK-01 to FK-42 range, the matrix records two things: whether it is implemented in the deployed codebase, and whether its behaviour was verified during development. ``Verified during development'' is a narrower claim than passing an automated test suite, and it is the honest one to make: thirty-six of the thirty-seven in-scope functional requirements are implemented and developer-verified, one is partial (FK-30, driving and rest-time status), and the five out-of-scope requirements (FK-38 through FK-42) are documented as future work. The absence of a formal automated test suite is itself a non-functional gap, named as L9 in \Cref{sec:limitations}. The traceability matrix's role is to make coverage visible, not to substitute for the testing that L9 acknowledges is missing.
9d978b7b68a9873b.summary: The requirements traceability matrix records implementation and developer-verified behaviour for each functional requirement, making coverage visible.

b99dda6ef6688323.paragraph: Relevance and validity bound the interview component first. The seven coordinators were a purposive sample matched to the research question, which asks about coordinator experience of the visibility gap rather than its prevalence in Norwegian transport. \textcite[p.~485]{malterud2001lancet} treats purposive sampling as the appropriate strategy for qualitative inquiry. Validity within that sample rests on triangulation across the seven calls: the visibility gap and the operator-vs-owner asymmetry surfaced across companies of different size and system maturity rather than from any single coordinator. The findings transfer in Malterud's bounded sense of applicability within a specified setting rather than to the population at large \parencite[p.~486]{malterud2001lancet}, and the bounds are named as L1 (sample size, brief duration) and L2 (self-selection from Admmit's customer roster) in \Cref{sec:limitations}.
b99dda6ef6688323.summary: Relevance and validity bound the interview component through purposive sampling and triangulation across the seven calls.

b8d106c4e58c3303.paragraph: Validity for the system component is narrower. Two instruments carry it, both set out in \Cref{sec:evaluation-framework}: the requirements traceability matrix that records implementation and developer-verified behaviour for each functional requirement, and the multi-engine benchmark that compares the three engines on identical synthetic instances. Together they validate the artefact in Wieringa's sense (predicting how it would behave once deployed) rather than evaluating it in deployment (see \Cref{sec:dsr}). The gaps that bound this validation (no production deployment, no user testing of the override flow, no automated test suite) are forwarded as L6, L8, and L9 in \Cref{sec:limitations}.
b8d106c4e58c3303.summary: Validity for the system component rests on the requirements traceability matrix and the multi-engine benchmark together.
